citation.title: Average treatment effects in the presence of unknown interference

standing_assumptions: [Setting: Section 3.1, p. 676 (PDF p. 4)] Consider a sample of $n$ units indexed by the set $\mathbf{U} = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. An experimenter intervenes on the world in ways that potentially affect the units. The intervention is described by a $n$-dimensional binary vector $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n) \in \{0, 1\}^n$. For short, we refer to $z_i$ as unit $i$'s treatment. Each unit has a function $y_i : \{0, 1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ denoting the observed outcome for the unit under a specific and potentially counterfactual intervention. In particular, $y_i(\mathbf{z})$ is the response of $i$ when the intervention is $\mathbf{z}$. We refer to the elements of the image of this function as potential outcomes. Let $\mathbf{z}_{-i} = (z_1, \ldots, z_{i-1}, z_{i+1}, \ldots, z_n)$ denote the $(n-1)$-dimensional vector constructed by deleting the $i$th element from $\mathbf{z}$. The potential outcome $y_i(\mathbf{z})$ can then be written as $y_i(z_i; \mathbf{z}_{-i})$. Throughout the paper, we assume that the potential outcomes are well-defined. The experimenter sets $\mathbf{z}$ according to a random vector $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n)$. The probability distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ is the design of the experiment. The design is the sole source of randomness we will consider. Let $Y_i$ denote the observed outcome of unit $i$: $Y_i = y_i(\mathbf{Z})$. As above, $\mathbf{Z}_{-i}$ denotes $\mathbf{Z}$ without its $i$th element, so $Y_i = y_i(Z_i; \mathbf{Z}_{-i})$. [No interference: Section 3.2, p. 676 (PDF p. 4)] It is conventional to assume that the potential outcomes are restricted so a unit's outcome is only affected by its own treatment. That is, for any two assignments $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{z}'$, if the treatment of a given unit is the same for both assignments, then the outcome for that unit is also the same. This no-interference assumption admits a definition of the treatment effect $\tau_i$ for unit $i$: $\tau_i = y_i(1; \mathbf{z}_{-i}) - y_i(0; \mathbf{z}_{-i})$, where $\mathbf{z}_{-i}$ is any element of $\{0, 1\}^{n-1}$. [Definitions 1 to 3: p. 677 (PDF p. 5)] DEFINITION 1. Under no interference, the average treatment effect (ATE) is the average unit-level treatment effect: $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tau_i$. The assignment-conditional unit-level treatment effect is $\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i}) = y_i(1; \mathbf{z}_{-i}) - y_i(0; \mathbf{z}_{-i})$. DEFINITION 2. An assignment-conditional average treatment effect is the average of the assignment-conditional unit-level treatment effects under a given assignment: $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})$. DEFINITION 3. The expected average treatment effect (EATE) is the expected assignment-conditional average treatment effect: $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \mathrm{E}[\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{Z})]$, where the expectation is taken over the distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ given by the experimental design. [Definition 4: p. 678 (PDF p. 6)] DEFINITION 4. The average distributional shift effect (ADSE) is the average difference between the conditional expected outcomes for the two treatment conditions: $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\mathrm{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathrm{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 0]\right)$. [Interference indicator: Section 4, p. 680 (PDF p. 8)] We say that unit $i$ interferes with unit $j$ if changing $i$'s treatment changes $j$'s outcome under at least one treatment assignment. We also say that a unit interferes with itself even if its own treatment does not affect its outcome. The indicator $I_{ij}$ denotes such interference: $I_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } y_j(\mathbf{z}) \ne y_j(\mathbf{z}') \text{ for some } \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}' \in \{0, 1\}^n \text{ such that } \mathbf{z}_{-i} = \mathbf{z}'_{-i}, \\ 1 & \text{if } i = j, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$ [Definition 5 (Interference dependence): p. 681 (PDF p. 9)] $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} d_{ij}$ where $d_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } I_{\ell i} I_{\ell j} = 1 \text{ for some } \ell \in \mathbf{U}, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$ The sum $d_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} d_{ij}$ gives the number of interference dependencies for unit $i$. [Interference counts: p. 681 (PDF p. 9)] $c_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} I_{ij}$ and $C_p = \left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^p\right]^{1/p}$. We write $C_\infty$ for the limit of $C_p$ as $p \to \infty$, which is the maximum $c_i$ over $\mathbf{U}$. [Asymptotic regime: Section 5, pp. 681–682 (PDF pp. 9–10)] We consider an arbitrary sequence of samples indexed by their sample size. The samples are not assumed to be drawn from some larger population or otherwise randomly generated. All quantities describing the samples, such as the potential outcomes and experimental designs, have their own sequences also indexed by $n$. But we leave the indexing implicit as no confusion arises. [Definition 6: p. 682 (PDF p. 10)] The Horvitz–Thompson (HT) and Hájek (HÁ) estimators are $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Z_i Y_i}{p_i} - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{(1 - Z_i)Y_i}{1 - p_i}$ and $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Z_i Y_i}{p_i} \Big/ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Z_i}{p_i}\right) - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{(1 - Z_i)Y_i}{1 - p_i} \Big/ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1 - Z_i}{1 - p_i}\right)$, where $p_i = \Pr(Z_i = 1)$ is the marginal treatment probability for unit $i$. [Assumption 1: p. 682 (PDF p. 10)] We assume throughout the remainder of the paper that the experimental design and potential outcomes are sufficiently well behaved, as formalized in the following assumption. ASSUMPTION 1 (Regularity conditions). There exist constants $k < \infty$, $q \ge 2$ and $s \ge 1$ such that for all $i \in \mathbf{U}$ in the sequence of samples: A (Probabilistic assignment). $k^{-1} \le \Pr(Z_i = 1) \le 1 - k^{-1}$, B (Outcome moments). $\mathrm{E}[|Y_i|^q] \le k^q$, C (Potential outcome moments). $\mathrm{E}[|y_i(z; \mathbf{Z}_{-i})|^s] \le k^s$ for $z \in \{0, 1\}$. [Assumption 2: p. 683 (PDF p. 11)] ASSUMPTION 2 (Restricted interference). $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} = o(n)$. [Bernoulli design: p. 683 (PDF p. 11)] We call this a Bernoulli randomization design, and it satisfies $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i^{z_i}(1 - p_i)^{1 - z_i}$ for some set of assignment probabilities $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$ bounded away from zero and one. [Complete randomization: p. 684 (PDF p. 12)] $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \begin{cases} \binom{n}{m}^{-1} & \text{if } \sum_{i=1}^{n} z_i = m, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases}$ where $m = \lfloor pn \rfloor$ for some fixed $p$ strictly between zero and one. We call the design complete randomization. [Paired randomization: p. 685 (PDF p. 13)] It is implicit that the sample size is even so that all units are paired. Let $\rho : \mathbf{U} \to \mathbf{U}$ describe a pairing so that $\rho(i) = j$ indicates that units $i$ and $j$ are paired. The pairing is symmetric, so the self-composition of $\rho$ is the identity function. The paired randomization design then satisfies $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \begin{cases} 2^{-n/2} & \text{if } z_i \ne z_{\rho(i)} \text{ for all } i \in \mathbf{U}, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$ [Notation the paper uses without defining] The paper does not define $\mathcal{O}_p$, $o_p$, 'consistent' or 'root-$n$ consistent'. The proof of Lemma A5 (Supplement A, p. 4) uses $X_n - x_n = \mathcal{O}_p(a_n)$ in the sense that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there are a constant $\kappa$ and an $N$ such that $\Pr(|X_n - x_n| \ge \kappa a_n) \le \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge N$. 'Consistent for' an estimand means that the difference between the estimator and the estimand (both sequences in $n$) converges in probability to zero; 'root-$n$ consistent' means that this difference is $\mathcal{O}_p(n^{-0.5})$. Supplement A is the separate file 'Supplement A: Proofs' (41 pp., DOI 10.1214/20-AOS1973SUPPA) and Supplement B is 'Supplement B: Simulation study' (21 pp., DOI 10.1214/20-AOS1973SUPPB); their page numbers are their own printed page numbers, which equal their PDF page numbers. In the main article the printed page number is the PDF page number plus 672.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proof of Lemma A23, first display, third line: the bound by the sum of $\alpha(Z_i, Z_j)$ over all pairs, corrected
canonical_claim.location: Supplement A, p. 23, proof of Lemma A23, first display
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected display] For any design, any $z \in \{0, 1\}$ and any $k > 0$: $\frac{k^2}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\left[\Pr(Z_i = z, Z_j = z) - \Pr(Z_i = z)\Pr(Z_j = z)\right] \le \frac{k^2}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\alpha(Z_i, Z_j) \le \frac{k^2 d_{\mathrm{AVG}}}{n} + \frac{k^2}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(1 - d_{ij})\alpha(Z_i, Z_j)$. The first inequality holds term by term, for every pair including $i = j$, by the definition of the alpha-mixing coefficient applied to the events $\{Z_i = z\}$ and $\{Z_j = z\}$. The second uses $d_{ij} + (1 - d_{ij}) = 1$, $0 \le \alpha(Z_i, Z_j) \le \frac{1}{4}$ and $\sum_{i,j} d_{ij} = n d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$; the diagonal terms are covered by $d_{ii} = 1$. Equivalently, keep the sum over $j \ne i$ and add $\frac{k^2}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Pr(Z_i = z)(1 - \Pr(Z_i = z))$. The final bound of the display and Lemma A23 are unchanged.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the setting, $y_i$, $\mathbf{Z}$, $Y_i$ (p. 676); $\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}$ (p. 677); $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}}$ (p. 678); $I_{ij}$ (p. 680); $d_{ij}$, $d_i$, $d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$, $c_i$, $C_p$, $C_\infty$ (p. 681); $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}}$, $p_i$, Assumption 1 (p. 682); Assumption 2 and the Bernoulli design (p. 683); complete randomization (p. 684); paired randomization (p. 685); the senses of $\mathcal{O}_p$ and 'consistent'. [Definition A1 and Corollary A1: Supplement A, p. 2] DEFINITION A1. $\mu_z = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{E}[y_i(z; \mathbf{Z}_{-i})]$, $\breve\mu_z = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{E}[y_i(z; \mathbf{Z}_{-i}) \mid Z_i = z]$, $\hat\mu_z = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\mathbb{1}[Z_i = z]Y_i}{\Pr(Z_i = z)}$, $\hat n_z = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\mathbb{1}[Z_i = z]}{\Pr(Z_i = z)}$. COROLLARY A1. $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \mu_1 - \mu_0$, $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}} = \breve\mu_1 - \breve\mu_0$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} = \hat\mu_1 - \hat\mu_0$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} = \frac{n}{\hat n_1}\hat\mu_1 - \frac{n}{\hat n_0}\hat\mu_0$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}} = (\hat\mu_1 - \breve\mu_1) - (\hat\mu_0 - \breve\mu_0)$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} - \tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}} = \left(\frac{n}{\hat n_1}\hat\mu_1 - \breve\mu_1\right) - \left(\frac{n}{\hat n_0}\hat\mu_0 - \breve\mu_0\right)$. [Assignment vectors affecting a unit: p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i = (I_{1i}Z_1, I_{2i}Z_2, \ldots, I_{ni}Z_n)$. The vector is defined so that its $j$th element is $Z_j$ if unit $j$ is interfering with $i$, and zero otherwise. Let $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i}$ be the $(n-1)$-dimensional vector constructed by deleting the $i$th element from $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i$. The definitions have the following convenient properties: $Y_i = y_i(\mathbf{Z}) = y_i(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i)$ and $y_i(z; \mathbf{Z}_{-i}) = y_i(z; \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i})$. [Alpha-mixing coefficient: p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] For two random variables $X$ and $Y$ defined on the same probability space, let $\alpha(X, Y) = \sup_{x \in \sigma(X),\, y \in \sigma(Y)} \left|\Pr(x \cap y) - \Pr(x)\Pr(y)\right|$, where $\sigma(X)$ and $\sigma(Y)$ denote the sub-sigma-algebras generated by the random variables. The coefficient $\alpha(X, Y)$ is zero if and only if $X$ and $Y$ are independent. The maximum is $\alpha(X, Y) = 1/4$. [Definition 9 (External and internal average mixing coefficients): p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] For the maximum values of $q$ and $s$ such that Assumptions 1B and 1C hold, let $\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(1 - d_{ij})\left[\alpha(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i, \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_j)\right]^{\frac{q-2}{q}}$ and $\alpha_{\mathrm{INT}} = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\alpha(Z_i, \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i})\right]^{\frac{s-1}{s}}$, where $0^0$ is defined as zero to accommodate the cases $q = 2$ and $s = 1$. [Assumptions 5 and 6: p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] ASSUMPTION 5 (Design mixing). $\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}} = o(n)$. ASSUMPTION 6 (Design separation). $\alpha_{\mathrm{INT}} = o(n)$.
canonical_claim.note: Sol's smallest repair: replace $\sum_{j \ne i}$ by $\sum_{j=1}^{n}$ in the middle sum. The first step of the same display (the replacement of the weights by $k^2$ inside a signed sum) is the separate finding P009-E009, whose corrected chain for Lemma A23 starts from absolute covariances and reaches the same final bound.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proof of Lemma A12: the hypergeometric laws of $T_i$ and the identity for the likelihood ratio that follows from them, as printed
canonical_claim.location: Supplement A, p. 10, proof of Lemma A12: the two probability displays after 'hyper-geometric according to:' and the displays that follow. Lemma A12 and Definition A3: p. 9
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed step] [Supplement A, p. 10] We have $T_i \le \reflectbox{c}_i \le \min(m, n - m)$, which, together with complete randomization, implies that $T_i$ is hyper-geometric according to: $\Pr(T_i = t) = \binom{m}{t}\binom{n - m}{\reflectbox{c}_i - t}\binom{n}{\reflectbox{c}_i}^{-1}$, $\Pr(T_i = t \mid Z_i = z) = z\binom{m - 1}{t}\binom{n - m}{\reflectbox{c}_i - t}\binom{n - 1}{\reflectbox{c}_i}^{-1} + (1 - z)\binom{m}{t}\binom{n - m - 1}{\reflectbox{c}_i - t}\binom{n - 1}{\reflectbox{c}_i}^{-1}$. [...] so we have: $\frac{\Pr(T_i = t \mid Z_i = z)}{\Pr(T_i = t)} - 1 = \frac{\reflectbox{c}_i}{\Pr(Z_i = z)(n - \reflectbox{c}_i)}\left[\Pr(Z_i = z) - z\frac{t}{\reflectbox{c}_i} - (1 - z)\frac{\reflectbox{c}_i - t}{\reflectbox{c}_i}\right]$, where the last equality exploits that $n\Pr(Z_i = z) = zm + (1 - z)(n - m)$ under complete randomization. [What is refuted] The two printed laws and the printed identity for the ratio: $T_i$ counts treated units among the $\reflectbox{c}_i - 1$ units other than $i$ that interfere with $i$, so the number of draws is $\reflectbox{c}_i - 1$, not $\reflectbox{c}_i$. The inequality stated in Lemma A12 is not refuted. [Counterexample, from the validator] $n = 4$, $m = 2$ (complete randomization, six assignments of probability $\frac{1}{6}$), $i = 1$, $y_1(\mathbf{v}) = v_1 + v_2$ and $y_j(\mathbf{v}) = v_j$ for $j = 2, 3, 4$. Then $I_{11} = I_{21} = 1$ and $I_{31} = I_{41} = 0$, so $\reflectbox{c}_1 = 2 = \min(m, n - m)$ and $T_1 = Z_2$. For $t = 0, 1, 2$: the true $\Pr(T_1 = t)$ is $(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}, 0)$, the printed formula gives $(\frac{1}{6}, \frac{2}{3}, \frac{1}{6})$; the true $\Pr(T_1 = t \mid Z_1 = 1)$ is $(\frac{2}{3}, \frac{1}{3}, 0)$, the printed formula gives $(\frac{1}{3}, \frac{2}{3}, 0)$; the true $\Pr(T_1 = t \mid Z_1 = 0)$ is $(\frac{1}{3}, \frac{2}{3}, 0)$, the printed formula gives $(0, \frac{2}{3}, \frac{1}{3})$. At $t = 0$, $z = 1$ the true ratio is $\frac{2/3}{1/2} = \frac{4}{3}$, while the printed laws give $\frac{1/3}{1/6} = 2$. [Second instance] $n = 4$, $m = 2$, $y_j(\mathbf{v}) = v_j$ for all $j$ (no interference): $\reflectbox{c}_i = 1$ and $T_i = 0$ surely, but the printed formula gives $\Pr(T_i = 0) = \binom{2}{0}\binom{2}{1}\binom{4}{1}^{-1} = \frac{1}{2}$.

The vector is defined so that its $j$th element is $Z_j$ if unit $j$ is interfering with $i$, and zero otherwise. Let $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i}$ be the $(n-1)$-dimensional vector constructed by deleting the $i$th element from $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i$. The definitions have the following convenient properties: $Y_i = y_i(\mathbf{Z}) = y_i(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i)$ and $y_i(z; \mathbf{Z}_{-i}) = y_i(z; \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i})$. [Alpha-mixing coefficient: p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] For two random variables $X$ and $Y$ defined on the same probability space, let $\alpha(X, Y) = \sup_{x \in \sigma(X),\, y \in \sigma(Y)} \left|\Pr(x \cap y) - \Pr(x)\Pr(y)\right|$, where $\sigma(X)$ and $\sigma(Y)$ denote the sub-sigma-algebras generated by the random variables. The coefficient $\alpha(X, Y)$ is zero if and only if $X$ and $Y$ are independent. The maximum is $\alpha(X, Y) = 1/4$. [Definition 9 (External and internal average mixing coefficients): p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] For the maximum values of $q$ and $s$ such that Assumptions 1B and 1C hold, let $\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(1 - d_{ij})\left[\alpha(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i, \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_j)\right]^{\frac{q-2}{q}}$ and $\alpha_{\mathrm{INT}} = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\alpha(Z_i, \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i})\right]^{\frac{s-1}{s}}$, where $0^0$ is defined as zero to accommodate the cases $q = 2$ and $s = 1$. [Definitions A2 and A3: Supplement A, p. 9] DEFINITION A2. Let $m = \sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i$ be the element sum of $\mathbf{Z}$ (i.e., the number of treated units). REMARK. Complete randomization implies that $m = \lfloor pn \rfloor$ with probability one for some fixed $p$ strictly between zero and one. DEFINITION A3. Let $\reflectbox{c}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} I_{ji}$ be the number of units interfering with unit $i$. (The paper prints this symbol as a reflected italic $c$; it is written $\reflectbox{c}_i$ here.) [Lemma A12: Supplement A, p. 9] Under complete randomization, for any $i \in \mathbf{U}$ such that $\reflectbox{c}_i \le \min(m, n - m)$ and any $z \in \{0, 1\}$: $\max_{\mathbf{z} \in \widetilde{\mathcal{Z}}_{-i}}\left|\frac{\Pr(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i} = \mathbf{z} \mid Z_i = z)}{\Pr(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i} = \mathbf{z})} - 1\right| \le \frac{\reflectbox{c}_i}{\Pr(Z_i = z)\min(m, n - m)}$, where $\widetilde{\mathcal{Z}}_{-i} = \{\mathbf{z} \in \{0, 1\}^{n-1} : \Pr(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i} = \mathbf{z}) > 0\}$ is the support of $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i}$. [From the proof: Supplement A, p. 9] Let $t_i(\mathbf{z}) = \sum_{j \ne i} I_{ji}z_j$ be the element sum of $\mathbf{z} \in \widetilde{\mathcal{Z}}_{-i}$, and let $T_i = \sum_{j \ne i} I_{ji}Z_j$ be the element sum of $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i}$ (i.e., the number of treated units interfering with $i$, excluding $i$ itself). [pp. 9-10] $\frac{\Pr(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i} = \mathbf{z} \mid Z_i = z)}{\Pr(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i} = \mathbf{z})} = \frac{\Pr(T_i = t_i(\mathbf{z}) \mid Z_i = z)}{\Pr(T_i = t_i(\mathbf{z}))}$.
canonical_claim.note: Rated an error, Minor. In the first instance the bound asserted by Lemma A12 is $\frac{2}{(1/2) \cdot 2} = 2$, and the true maximum of $|\text{ratio} - 1|$ is $\frac{1}{3}$, so the lemma holds there. The intermediate displays on p. 10 write $T$ for $T_i$ in two places.
